titleEn: The LORD is my light and my salvation
progression: | Em Em | Am Am | C D | Em Em |
intro: Fourteen verses in two tempers. The first six speak about God with complete confidence; from verse 7 the same voice turns and asks, and the imperatives arrive one after another: hear, be gracious, answer, do not hide, do not abandon me. Many communities say it morning and evening from the start of Elul through Hoshana Rabbah, so it is the psalm a learner meets most often in the weeks around the New Year. Watch the seam between verse 6 and verse 7. The Hebrew does nothing to soften it.

stichs.en: Of David.
The LORD is my light and my salvation; whom should I fear?
The LORD is the stronghold of my life; of whom should I be afraid?

verses.summary: The thesis arrives as two rhetorical questions rather than as a claim. Light and stronghold are the two registers the rest of the psalm works in: seeing, and being sheltered.

stichs.en: When evildoers drew near against me to devour my flesh,
my foes and my enemies against me, they are the ones who stumbled and fell.

verses.summary: The first threat is put in the past tense before it is described. Whatever came to devour is already the subject of a verb of falling.

stichs.en: If an army encamps against me, my heart will not fear.
If war rises against me, in this I stay confident.

verses.summary: The threat scales up from individuals to an army, and the answer stays exactly the same size. The heart is named as the organ that would do the fearing, and it does not.

stichs.en: One thing I have asked of the LORD, that is what I seek:
that I may dwell in the house of the LORD all the days of my life,
to gaze on the delight of the LORD and to visit in His sanctuary.

verses.summary: Everything narrows to a single request, and the request is not rescue. What is asked for is residence, and the two verbs at the end are about looking, not about being defended.

stichs.en: For He will hide me in His shelter on a day of trouble,
He will conceal me in the cover of His tent,
He will lift me high on a rock.

verses.summary: The reason clause for verse 4. Three images of covering, and the last one reverses direction: hidden low, then set up high on rock.

stichs.en: And now my head is lifted above my enemies around me,
and I will offer in His tent sacrifices with loud shouting,
I will sing, I will make music to the LORD.

verses.summary: The confident half closes on sound: head lifted, shouting, singing. The enemies have not been removed, they are still standing all around him.

stichs.en: Hear, LORD, my voice when I call,
and be gracious to me and answer me.

verses.summary: The hinge of the psalm. The speaker who needed nothing in verse 1 now asks to be heard, and from here every main verb is an imperative.

stichs.en: Of You my heart said: seek My face.
Your face, LORD, I will seek.

verses.summary: A quotation inside a prayer. The heart repeats a command addressed to a plural you, and the speaker then answers it in the singular, for himself.

stichs.en: Do not hide Your face from me,
do not turn Your servant away in anger.
You have been my help;
do not abandon me and do not forsake me, God of my salvation.

verses.summary: Five negative petitions in a row. What is feared is no longer defeat but abandonment, which is the exact opposite of the face the speaker asked to look at in verse 8.

stichs.en: Though my father and my mother have left me,
the LORD will gather me in.

verses.summary: The extreme case, offered as an argument rather than as a complaint. If the two people who by definition do not abandon you did, the claim of verse 1 still holds.

stichs.en: Teach me Your way, LORD,
and lead me on a level path,
because of those who lie in wait for me.

verses.summary: The request shifts from protection to instruction. Being taught a level path is treated here as the practical form of being kept safe.

stichs.en: Do not hand me over to the appetite of my foes,
for false witnesses have risen against me, and one who breathes out violence.

verses.summary: The enemies are named for the first time as witnesses rather than as soldiers. The danger has moved off the battlefield and into a court.

stichs.en: Were it not that I trusted I would see
the goodness of the LORD in the land of the living.

verses.summary: A sentence that never finishes. The condition is stated and the consequence is left unsaid, and the Masoretic scribes marked the opening word with dots above the letters.

stichs.en: Wait for the LORD.
Be strong and let your heart take courage.
And wait for the LORD.

verses.summary: Someone answers, or the speaker answers himself. The verb of waiting frames the line at both ends, and nothing at all is promised in between.

pardes.body: Two psalms' worth of mood in one text. Verses 1 to 6 are declarative and speak of God in the third person: light, stronghold, shelter, rock, and an enemy who has already fallen. From verse 7 nearly every main verb is an imperative addressed directly to God, and most of the requests are negative: do not hide, do not turn away, do not abandon, do not hand me over. Because of this, many scholars treat the halves as two originally separate poems joined later, while others read the change as the whole point, a person saying what he believes and then discovering he still has to ask for it. The Hebrew offers no seam to point at, so the question stays open. Notice {{6.0}}, and now, which closes the confident half by pulling it into the present tense.

The psalm is built on eyes and faces. {{1.2}}, my light, makes seeing the governing image, and it comes back at {{4.13}}, to gaze on the delight of the LORD, and again at {{13.2}}, to see. Against that, the whole petition half is afraid of a face being hidden. {{4.15}} is a genuine crux: the root can mean to visit, to inspect, or to seek out, and the 1917 Jewish Publication Society rendering, to visit early in His temple, hears in it the word for morning instead. The word at {{13.0}} carries the Masoretic extraordinary points, dots written above the letters, and the sentence it opens has no ending at all: the condition is given, the consequence is never stated, and translators have to supply one or leave the line hanging.

The custom of saying this psalm twice a day from the start of Elul through the festival season is usually explained by a reading that hears the calendar inside it: my light for the New Year, and my salvation for the Day of Atonement, and He will hide me in His shelter for the festival of booths, since {{5.2}} is written with the same consonants as the word for that booth. Which came first, the custom or the reading, is not clear from the sources, and the practice is attested far later than the psalm. Verse 10 has its own afterlife in Jewish reading, where the father and mother who leave are taken less as a biography of David than as the limit case that makes the argument work: the psalm names the one abandonment nobody expects, in order to say that the claim survives it.

Read mystically the psalm is one movement, not two. The first half is what a soul knows while the light is on it; the second is the same soul when the light withdraws, and the withdrawal is not punishment but the condition that makes asking possible. {{5.2}} is a shelter that hides, and hiding is treated here as a form of nearness rather than distance, which is why the worst thing the speaker can name in verse 9 is a face turned away and the best thing he can name in verse 4 is a face he is allowed to look at. {{14.0}}, wait, is the verb of the space between the two states, and it is said twice in a single line, as though the waiting had to be doubled to be survivable.
